units.sourceHTML: 6.3 Multiline techniques - using D,G,H,N,P to process multiple lines

units.text: Multiple lines can be processed as one buffer using the ⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧,⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧,⟦4⟧. They are similar to their lowercase counterparts (⟦5⟧,⟦6⟧, ⟦7⟧,⟦8⟧,⟦9⟧), except that these commands append or subtract data while respecting embedded newlines - allowing adding and removing lines from the pattern and hold spaces.
units.sourceHTML: Multiple lines can be processed as one buffer using the D,G,H,N,P. They are similar to their lowercase counterparts (d,g, h,n,p), except that these commands append or subtract data while respecting embedded newlines - allowing adding and removing lines from the pattern and hold spaces.

units.text: ⟦0⟧deletes⟦1⟧ line from the pattern space until the first newline, and restarts the cycle.
units.sourceHTML: deletes line from the pattern space until the first newline, and restarts the cycle.

units.text: ⟦0⟧appends⟦1⟧ line from the hold space to the pattern space, with a newline before it.
units.sourceHTML: appends line from the hold space to the pattern space, with a newline before it.

units.text: ⟦0⟧appends⟦1⟧ line from the pattern space to the hold space, with a newline before it.
units.sourceHTML: appends line from the pattern space to the hold space, with a newline before it.

units.text: ⟦0⟧appends⟦1⟧ line from the input file to the pattern space.
units.sourceHTML: appends line from the input file to the pattern space.

units.text: ⟦0⟧prints⟦1⟧ line from the pattern space until the first newline.
units.sourceHTML: prints line from the pattern space until the first newline.

units.text: ⟦0⟧ starts by reading the first line into the pattern space (i.e. ‘⟦1⟧’).
units.sourceHTML: • sed starts by reading the first line into the pattern space (i.e. ‘1’).

units.text: At the beginning of every cycle, the ⟦0⟧ command appends a newline and the next line to the pattern space (i.e. ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, ‘⟦3⟧’ in the first cycle).
units.sourceHTML: • At the beginning of every cycle, the N command appends a newline and the next line to the pattern space (i.e. ‘1’, ‘\n’, ‘2’ in the first cycle).

units.text: The ⟦0⟧ command prints the content of the pattern space unambiguously.
units.sourceHTML: • The l command prints the content of the pattern space unambiguously.

units.text: The ⟦0⟧ command then removes the content of pattern space up to the first newline (leaving ‘⟦1⟧’ at the end of the first cycle).
units.sourceHTML: • The D command then removes the content of pattern space up to the first newline (leaving ‘2’ at the end of the first cycle).

units.text: At the next cycle the ⟦0⟧ command appends a newline and the next input line to the pattern space (e.g. ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, ‘⟦3⟧’).
units.sourceHTML: • At the next cycle the N command appends a newline and the next input line to the pattern space (e.g. ‘2’, ‘\n’, ‘3’).

units.text: The first expression, ⟦0⟧ operates on all non-empty lines, and adds the current line (in the pattern space) to the hold space. On all lines except the last, the pattern space is deleted and the cycle is restarted.
units.sourceHTML: • The first expression, /./{H;$!d} operates on all non-empty lines, and adds the current line (in the pattern space) to the hold space. On all lines except the last, the pattern space is deleted and the cycle is restarted.

units.text: The other expressions ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ are executed only on empty lines (i.e. paragraph separators). The ⟦2⟧ command fetches the accumulated lines from the hold space back to the pattern space. The ⟦3⟧ command then operates on all the text in the paragraph (including the embedded newlines).
units.sourceHTML: • The other expressions x and s are executed only on empty lines (i.e. paragraph separators). The x command fetches the accumulated lines from the hold space back to the pattern space. The s/// command then operates on all the text in the paragraph (including the embedded newlines).
